nature-nbs-019.title: The urban heat island: why cities run hot
nature-nbs-019.text: In the 1810s Luke Howard reported that central London was 2.1 °C warmer at night than the surrounding countryside. He had found the urban heat island effect: cities become noticeably warmer than the land around them. The main cause is how cities change land surfaces. Dark materials like asphalt and concrete absorb much more sunlight and store its heat, so city surfaces warm faster than rural ones. Waste heat from energy use adds a little more. The gap is usually biggest at night and clearest when winds are weak. It matters to a lot of people. Urban areas cover about 0.5% of Earth's land but hold more than half the world's people. Heat islands can lengthen and intensify heat waves, raise demand for air conditioning and warm streams fed by hot stormwater. Climate change does not cause the effect, but it amplifies it. The remedies are well known. They include planting trees, white or reflective roofs, light-colored concrete, planted roofs and passive radiative cooling, surfaces that shed heat to the sky.

nature-nbs-009.title: Urban green space: country in the city
nature-nbs-009.text: Around the first century C.E., the Romans had a phrase for it: 'rus in urbe', country in the city. In town planning, urban green spaces are open areas set aside for parks and other greenery. The World Health Organization defines them more broadly, as all city land covered by vegetation of any kind. They include plant life and water features, called blue spaces, and range from playing fields to wilder-looking land. Their benefits fall into four groups: recreation, ecology, beauty and health. Green spaces can clean city air, shelter wildlife and lower flood risk by draining rainwater. Homes near urban open spaces tend to be worth more. Quality matters as much as quantity. Visitors gain more from green spaces with more biodiversity, so variety counts, not just greenness.

nature-nbs-001.title: Green roofs: gardens on top of buildings
nature-nbs-001.text: Even 19 stories up, a green roof can attract bees, butterflies, birds and other helpful insects. A green roof is a roof partly or fully covered with plants and a growing medium, laid over a waterproof membrane. It may also have a root barrier, drainage layers and irrigation. The benefits stack up. Green roofs add mass and insulation, cutting energy use, and they ease the urban heat island by raising evapotranspiration. A study cited by the US EPA found they reduced rainwater runoff by over 75% during rainstorms. The plants store carbon in their tissue and, through litter and roots, in the soil. Shielding the membrane from sunlight and damage can extend a roof's life by over 200%. The catch is cost. An extensive system can cost $108–$248/m2 and an intensive one $355–$2,368/m2, and the up-front cost can be double that of a normal roof. Toronto approved a by-law in May 2009 requiring green roofs on residential and industrial buildings.

nature-nbs-016.title: Urban agriculture: farms inside the city
nature-nbs-016.text: Shipping food from far away used 4 to 17 times more fuel than local and regional transport, one study found. Urban agriculture is the growing, processing and distribution of food in towns and cities. It includes raising animals, fish farming, beekeeping and horticulture, and differs from peri-urban farming at the rural edge of suburbs. Its two main types are gardens and farms; the USDA counts as a farm any place that produces and sells $1,000 or more of farm products. City farming supplies fresh produce, jobs and income, and can improve food security and nutrition. Urban farms can also act as carbon sinks where pavement and buildings outnumber plants. The obstacles are real. Old soils are often contaminated with lead and other heavy metals. City land is scarce and expensive, and irrigating with untreated wastewater can spread waterborne disease.

nature-nbs-022.title: Urban parks: shade, play and a cooler summer
nature-nbs-022.text: A 2025 satellite study of 2,083 parks found that well-treed parks were on average 3.4°C cooler on summer days than the city around them. An urban park is a park or garden in a town or suburb that gives residents and visitors green space and places to relax and play. Parks are usually designed landscapes rather than land left natural, and most are run by local government. Trees are chosen for beauty and shade, with growing focus on cooling the urban heat island. Early purpose-built public parks included Princes Park in Liverpool, opened in 1843, and Birkenhead Park, which Olmsted visited in 1850. As city land prices rose, most new US parks since the 1960s have been small pocket parks. The UK has about 27,000 public parks with around 2.6 billion visits a year, but councils have no legal duty to fund them.

nature-nbs-007.title: Urban forestry: trees as city infrastructure
nature-nbs-007.text: The United States has around 3.8 billion urban trees, with an estimated structural value of $2.4 trillion. Urban forestry is the care and management of trees in towns and cities to improve the urban environment. It treats trees as a vital part of a city's infrastructure, covering planting, care, protection and management as a shared resource. City trees filter air pollution, regulate local climate and store carbon dioxide. They cool the urban heat island by shading pavement, helping air move and through evapotranspiration. That shade saves lives: heat waves kill 1,300 people a year in the United States, more than any other weather event. City life is hard on trees, with cramped roots, poor soil, heat, pollution, physical damage and too much or too little water and light. Planners weigh their services against their disservices beforehand.

nature-nbs-005.title: Green walls: gardens that grow sideways
nature-nbs-005.text: In 1986 the French botanist Patrick Blanc built a large indoor wall of plants in Paris, and he is often credited with popularizing the idea. A green wall, living wall or vertical garden is an upright built structure deliberately covered with plants. Unlike a green facade, where climbers grow up from soil at the base, a green wall holds its growing medium on the wall itself. Plant surfaces cooled by transpiration stay no more than 4–5 °C above air temperature, so green walls lower building temperatures. They make good use of vertical space, and in dry areas their circulating water evaporates less than in flat gardens. Living walls are credited with cleaning air, and one computer model showed a wall absorbing nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter. Deeper substrates tend to support the most species. Walls are classed by growth medium: freestanding, media-free, loose, mat and structural.

nature-nbs-026.title: Green belts: a ring of countryside around the city
nature-nbs-026.text: In 1875 Octavia Hill first used the term green belt about London's growth, and the UK pioneered the policy. A green belt is a planning zone that keeps mostly undeveloped, wild or farmed land around or beside towns and cities. It works like an invisible border that blocks building and lets wildlife return. Its aims include protecting natural areas, cleaning city air, giving townspeople access to the countryside and keeping rural communities from being swallowed by suburbs. England's fourteen green belts cover 16,716 km2, or 12.4% of England. They are contested. Critics such as the Institute of Economic Affairs say green belts block new housing and push up house prices. Because a belt has an outer edge, building can leap over it, which may spread sprawl and lengthen commutes. Defenders point to the farming inside green belts, which stores carbon, cools cities and provides habitat.

nature-nbs-030.title: Urban forests: woods inside the city limits
nature-nbs-030.text: Johannesburg sits on naturally treeless grassland, yet it reportedly has 10 million planted trees and is often called the largest man-made urban forest. An urban forest is a forest or grove of trees growing inside a city, town or suburb. Unlike a forest park, it often lacks toilets, paved paths or clear borders. Urban forests moderate local climate, slow wind and stormwater, filter air and help cool the urban heat island. The numbers can be large. Models suggest 100 million trees in US cities could cut annual energy use by 30 billion kWh. That would save $2 billion and 9 million tons of power plant CO2 a year. A 40-year study in Tucson calculated $600,000 saved in stormwater treatment. A Finnish study found property values rose 4.9% for each kilometre closer to a forest. In Philadelphia, poor residents near 'greened' vacant lots reported a 68% fall in feelings of depression.

nature-nbs-010.title: Green space and health: why parks are medicine
nature-nbs-010.text: People living within 1 km of green space show lower risk of heart and blood vessel disease. The World Health Organization treats urban green space as important to mental and physical health. Green space encourages exercise and reduces air pollution, heat, traffic noise and emissions, all of which raise the risk of chronic and mental illness. The closer people live to parks, and the more land is parks, the fewer local treatments for anxiety and mood disorders. Areas with many trees have markedly lower levels of ozone, PM10, NO2, SO2 and CO. Children with more access to parks are more active, and green space is linked to better focus and working memory at school. Plant choice matters, though, because large tree canopies can add to asthma and allergies.

nature-nbs-011.title: Green space inequality: who gets the trees
nature-nbs-011.text: Neighborhoods with more minority residents often have less park access, a legacy of past redlining, when lenders refused loans in certain areas, and of present funding choices. Green space inequality is this uneven sharing of parks, trees and other green space. The parks that do exist in minority neighborhoods are often small, poorly kept, unsafe or unsuited to local needs. American Forests calls the tree version canopy inequity: fewer city trees in disadvantaged neighborhoods. The problem is growing. As cities become denser, more people, especially those on low incomes, live in less green surroundings.

nature-nbs-028.title: Urban ecology: studying nature among the buildings
nature-nbs-028.text: Ecologists largely turned to cities from the 1970s. Urban ecology is the scientific study of how living things relate to each other and to their surroundings in cities. Dense buildings and paved surfaces create a distinctive landscape. Its goal is a balance between human culture and the natural environment. Researchers use chemical tests, temperature records and heat maps, remote sensing and long-term research sites. Cities disturb nature's chemical cycles. Their demand for chemicals contributes to acid rain, eutrophication and global warming, while paving stops nutrients returning to the soil. Green infrastructure can make cities better homes for wildlife. Because the field is young, many effects of urban growth remain poorly understood.

nature-nbs-021.title: Cool roofs: painting the city white
nature-nbs-021.text: Cities are full of dark surfaces that soak up the sun's heat and lower the city's reflectiveness, its {{ref:nature-nbs-090}}. Painting rooftops white has become a common way to reduce the heat island effect. A newer option goes further. A passive daytime radiative cooling roof can double the energy savings of a white roof, most of all in hot, dry cities such as Phoenix and Las Vegas.

nature-nbs-020.title: Urban heat inequity: who swelters
nature-nbs-020.text: Heat does not spread evenly through a city. Urban heat inequity, or thermal inequity, is the uneven spread of heat that hits some communities harder than others. Heat stress often tracks race, ethnicity, income, education and age. In most US cities, people of color are more likely than white residents to live in the hottest areas. Past redlining shaped land use and still leaves trees and plants, and so heat, unevenly shared. Top-floor homes, dark roofs, poor insulation and unaffordable air conditioning make it worse for low-income households.

nature-nbs-003.title: Brown roofs: wasteland habitat moved upstairs
nature-nbs-003.text: Old industrial brownfield sites can be valuable ecosystems for rare plants, animals and invertebrates, but redevelopment threatens them. A brown or biodiverse roof offers a refuge. It covers the flat roof of a new building with locally sourced material to replace the wildlife habitat lost to the development below.

nature-nbs-002.title: Intensive or extensive: two kinds of green roof
nature-nbs-002.text: Green roofs are grouped as intensive, semi-intensive or extensive, by the depth of their planting medium and the upkeep they need. The difference in weight is large. Extensive roofs usually carry 50–120 kg/m2 of vegetation, while intensive roofs carry 390–730 kg/m2. Traditional roof gardens with deep soil for large plants or lawns count as intensive, because they need irrigation, feeding and other labor.

nature-nbs-013.title: Biophilic design: building nature back into daily life
nature-nbs-013.text: Peter Newman estimated that biophilic design could save New York City nearly $470 million through higher worker productivity and $1.7 billion through lower crime costs. Biophilic design tries to connect people more closely with nature, and with nature-like design, to improve their health and well-being. Stephen Kellert, a pioneer of the field, built a three-part framework. It covers direct experience of nature, indirect experience such as images and natural materials, and experience of space and place. The evidence is encouraging. In experiments, people recovered from stress faster and more fully in natural surroundings than urban ones. Plants, trees, rain gardens and green roofs also reduce hard surfaces, helping buildings manage stormwater. Natural elements can cost a little more to install and maintain, but their benefits are believed to outweigh this. The WELL Building Standard and the Living Building Challenge are its most prominent backers in building rating systems.

nature-nbs-031.title: Urban resilience: cities that bend without breaking
nature-nbs-031.text: A study of 616 cities, home to 1.7 billion people, found floods endanger more city residents than any other natural hazard, followed by earthquakes and storms. Urban resilience is a city's ability to withstand, recover from or adapt to human-made and natural disasters. It covers physical infrastructure as well as social, health and economic systems. Research has focused on climate change, natural disasters and terrorism. Greening is among the most cited heat strategies: plants cover heat-absorbing surfaces and shade concrete and asphalt. Replacing hard surfaces with greenery also lets soil and plants soak up excess rain, and deeper green roof soils absorb more. People matter as much as surfaces. Older people make up most heat-related deaths in cities, and social isolation adds to their risk. Since risk can never be fully removed, resilience means investing in options that work across uncertain futures.

nature-nbs-025.title: Blue roofs: storing the storm on top
nature-nbs-025.text: A blue roof is designed to store rainwater for a while and then release it slowly. Blue roofs are built on flat roofs in cities with too few permeable surfaces for rain to soak in. By easing the load on storm sewers, they help stop combined sewers overflowing untreated wastewater into rivers and coasts. Active blue roofs control drainage with valves, while passive ones slow water by lengthening its path to the drain. In dry climates they also save water by harvesting roof rainfall.

nature-nbs-004.title: Blue-green roofs: water below, plants above
nature-nbs-004.text: A blue-green roof combines a blue roof's water storage with a green roof's plants. It holds stormwater beneath layers of soil and vegetation. That reduces runoff, and the stored water can be reused to irrigate the plants above. The arrangement also cools the building inside.

nature-nbs-017.title: Community gardens: growing food and neighbors
nature-nbs-017.text: In many cities, residents garden on small plots and rooftops. A community garden is public space where residents grow plants for food, recreation and learning. The harvest is not only vegetables. Gardens often strengthen local social networks and give a neighborhood a focus that builds pride.

nature-nbs-018.title: Food deserts: where fresh food is hard to find
nature-nbs-018.text: In 2009 the USDA found good support for a troubling pattern: low-income and minority neighborhoods often have poor access to healthy food. Such places are called food deserts. Definitions vary, but US studies show racial gaps in the food environment. Urban farms can help. Those that sell fresh produce at affordable prices in food deserts can narrow the gap between rich and poor neighborhoods.

nature-nbs-023.title: Active and passive recreation: playing fields or quiet trails
nature-nbs-023.text: Park planners split space in two. Active recreation areas are built up for sports and play. Passive recreation areas keep open space and natural habitat. The costs differ sharply. Team sports need a lot of space, management, maintenance and money. Trails, benches and picnic areas need little management and can be provided very cheaply.

nature-nbs-024.title: Linear parks: long, thin and often on old railways
nature-nbs-024.text: A linear park is a park much longer than it is wide. A typical one is an old railway line turned into a rail trail or greenway, with the tracks removed and plants allowed back. New York's High Line is a North American example.

nature-nbs-033.title: Urban biodiversity: wildlife in the concrete
nature-nbs-033.text: Cities usually shrink nature's variety. They remove and fragment habitat and make once-distinct communities of species more alike. In temperate countries, urbanization often adds non-native species while cutting native ones, lowering overall species richness. Urban biodiversity is the variety of plant and animal life found in cities. Planners can sustain it. Enlarging green areas and linking them with a network of green corridors is a proven way to keep it high. Green roofs, tree inventories, hardy plantings and protected parks and woodlots all help. So do safe movement paths for wildlife, better habitat and fewer human threats.

nature-nbs-008.title: Street trees: the canopy along the curb
nature-nbs-008.text: A street tree is any tree growing along a city street, such as between the sidewalk and the curb. Because they grow among large paved areas, street trees make up an important share of a district's tree cover. They soak up stormwater, remove air pollutants and give shade that eases the urban heat island.

nature-nbs-032.title: Urban rewilding: letting wild nature into town
nature-nbs-032.text: Urban rewilding tries to bring working ecosystems, from plants to animals, into cities. It comes in four types: urban greening, corridors, small projects under 50 hectares and large projects over 50 hectares. Corridors such as restored waterways or green paths link habitats so city animals can move freely. The benefits include cleaner air, stored carbon, more pollination, fertile soil, clean water and lower stress. But projects are costly and carry an opportunity cost, since owners could use the land for more profitable purposes.

nature-nbs-015.title: Biophilic cities: places where people love their nature
nature-nbs-015.text: Singapore, nicknamed a 'city in a garden', built a network of nature reserves, parks, connectors and tree-lined streets to bring back wildlife and reduce urban heat. To Timothy Beatley, a biophilic city is one whose residents want to take part in, protect and connect with the nature around them. His framework judges cities by infrastructure, governance, knowledge and behavior, such as how many people live near a park. He argues biophilic design helps cities adapt to a changing climate.

nature-nbs-006.title: Pocket forests: dense, fast and disputed
nature-nbs-006.text: A pocket forest is a small forest made by planting many different native trees and shrubs close together, usually to restore native plants quickly. Instead of passing through early growth stages, it is planted densely with mature-stage species that race each other for sunlight. Interest grew largely from Japanese botanist Akira Miyawaki. The claims are disputed. Forestry scholars say claims that Miyawaki forests grow ten times faster are unsubstantiated, and call the method costly and unworkable for large areas. Dense, layered pocket forests can also catch embers and carry fire upward, raising wildfire risk in cities.

nature-nbs-027.title: Green urbanism: cities that give back
nature-nbs-027.text: In 1989 the ecologist H.T. Odum called cities 'parasites' that make no food and clean no air but only consume. Green urbanism answers that charge. It is the practice of building communities good for both people and the environment. Timothy Beatley describes it as shaping more sustainable places and lifestyles that use less of the world's resources. It treats urbanization as a key driver of carbon emissions, resource depletion and environmental damage, and aims for no fossil fuels, no waste and no emissions. It is interdisciplinary, drawing on planners, ecologists, engineers, economists, psychologists and others.

openers.cities-and-green-space: Cities run noticeably hotter than the countryside around them, and that heat falls hardest on poorer and minority neighborhoods, which often have fewer parks and trees. This chapter is about the green answers: parks, city forests, street trees, roofs and walls covered with plants, food grown in town, and belts of open land around the edges. The World Health Organization treats such green space as important to mental and physical health. Urban ecology, the study of how living things fare in cities, shows what each of these spaces can do.

reviews.cities-and-green-space: Cities trap heat, and green is the most cited remedy: trees, parks, green roofs and green walls shade surfaces and cool the air through evapotranspiration. The same plants soak up stormwater, clean the air, shelter wildlife and, as studies of health show, ease stress and protect hearts. The benefits are unevenly shared, with poorer and minority neighborhoods left hotter and less green, and food deserts showing the same pattern. Ideas from biophilic design to green urbanism try to build nature into the city for everyone, while debates over green belts and pocket forests show that greening still carries costs and trade-offs.
